questions.title: Site of vitamin D3 synthesis
questions.question: Synthesis of vit D3 occurs in ........... under the effect of..….

explanations.A: Incorrect. The eye has no role in vitamin D3 synthesis; there is no 7-dehydrocholesterol store or photochemical vitamin D pathway in ocular tissue. The eye's photoreceptors respond to light for vision, an entirely separate physiological process from steroid synthesis. Neither the organ nor the mechanism named here is correct.
explanations.B: Correct. Vitamin D3 synthesis begins in the skin, where ultraviolet B radiation converts a store of 7-dehydrocholesterol into pre-vitamin D3, which body heat then isomerises to vitamin D3 itself. Both the organ (skin) and the trigger (ultraviolet rays) named in this option match the actual pathway. Further activation to calcitriol happens later, in the liver and kidney, but the initial synthesis step is specifically in the skin under UV.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skin is the correct organ, but infrared rays do not carry the photon energy needed to drive the 7-dehydrocholesterol-to-pre-vitamin-D3 photochemical reaction; that reaction specifically requires UVB wavelengths. Infrared radiation is felt mainly as heat, not as a trigger for this photochemistry. This option gets the organ right but the trigger wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neither part of this option is correct — the eye is not the synthesis site, and infrared rays are not the trigger. Combining two wrong answers does not make a correct one. Both the organ and the mechanism are mismatched.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Skin is the correct organ, but visible light lacks the UV wavelength needed for the photochemical conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol. Only ultraviolet B radiation, not the visible spectrum, drives this specific reaction. This option again gets the organ right but the trigger wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin D3 synthesis begins in the skin under ultraviolet ray exposure.

questions.title: Primary function of melanin
questions.question: The primary function of melanin in the skin is to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin D synthesis depends on 7-dehydrocholesterol in keratinocytes reacting to UVB, a separate skin function from melanin's role. Melanin actually competes with this pathway by absorbing UV before it can trigger vitamin D synthesis. The two functions are related only in that both respond to UV exposure, not because melanin performs the synthesis itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Melanin's principal physiological role is absorbing and scattering ultraviolet radiation, which limits the UV-induced DNA photodamage that would otherwise accumulate in keratinocyte nuclei. Melanocytes transfer melanin to surrounding keratinocytes, where it forms a protective cap over the nucleus facing the skin surface. This is why individuals with less melanin carry higher UV-related skin damage and malignancy risk for the same sun exposure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skin temperature regulation depends on the sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels adjusting heat loss, not on melanin. Melanin has no direct thermoregulatory function. This option confuses two separate skin physiological roles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nitrogenous waste excretion is a kidney function, not a skin function at all, let alone one performed by melanin specifically. Skin plays only a minor, indirect role in excretion via sweat, and melanin has no part in that process.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Antimicrobial peptides such as cathelicidin and the defensins are produced by keratinocytes as a separate chemical defence mechanism, unrelated to melanin's pigment-based UV protection. These are two distinct skin defence systems, not the same function under different names.

questions.learning_objective: State that melanin's primary function is protecting skin cells from UV-induced DNA damage.

questions.title: Antimicrobial peptide from keratinocytes
questions.question: Which of the following antimicrobial peptides is produced by keratinocytes and acts against a broad spectrum of bacteria?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 'Sebumin' is not a recognised antimicrobial peptide; sebum itself (the oily secretion of sebaceous glands) has some antimicrobial properties from its component fatty acids, but it is not the peptide this question is describing. This option does not name a genuine keratinocyte-produced antimicrobial peptide.
explanations.B: Correct. Cathelicidin is an antimicrobial peptide produced by keratinocytes that disrupts the cell membranes of a broad range of bacteria, some fungi and enveloped viruses. It gives the skin surface constant, non-adaptive chemical defence without needing prior pathogen exposure. It is one of the two main families of skin antimicrobial peptides, alongside the defensins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ceramides are lipid molecules forming part of the stratum corneum's intercellular lipid matrix, contributing to the skin's mechanical/permeability barrier rather than acting as an antimicrobial peptide. They are structural lipids, not peptides with direct antibacterial action.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urocanic acid is a UV-absorbing breakdown product of the amino acid histidine found in the stratum corneum, contributing to UV protection rather than antimicrobial defence. It is not classified as an antimicrobial peptide.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Elastin is a structural protein giving skin its elastic recoil, found in the dermis, unrelated to antimicrobial defence. It has a purely mechanical/structural role, not a chemical defence one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cathelicidin as the keratinocyte-produced, broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptide.

questions.title: Normal core body temperature range
questions.question: The normal physiological range of core body temperature in humans is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This range sits below the normal core temperature band and would be considered mildly hypothermic if sustained. It does not match the range the hypothalamus normally defends. A person at these temperatures would typically show signs of cold stress.
explanations.B: Correct. Normal human core body temperature is physiologically maintained within a narrow range, classically cited as about 36.5-37.2°C, by the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre balancing heat production against heat loss. This is core (internal), not peripheral skin, temperature. The narrowness of this range is what makes deviations from it, such as fever, clinically meaningful.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This range is already in the low-grade fever territory, above the normal core temperature band. It would typically prompt evaluation for an underlying cause of elevated temperature rather than being considered a normal reading.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This range is well below normal core temperature and would represent a more significant degree of hypothermia if sustained. It does not correspond to the physiologically defended core range.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This range represents a clear fever, well above the normal core temperature band. It reflects a raised hypothalamic set point from illness or another pyrogenic stimulus, not the resting normal range.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal physiological range for human core body temperature.

questions.title: Substances that penetrate intact skin most readily
questions.question: Which of the following substances can penetrate the intact skin most readily?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Water-soluble ions are resisted by the lipid-rich stratum corneum, which is a poor medium for charged, hydrophilic particles to diffuse through. Their aqueous solubility works against them here, since the rate-limiting barrier layer is lipid-based, not water-based. They cross intact skin only with difficulty.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Large proteins are far too big and too hydrophilic to cross the tightly packed corneocyte/lipid architecture of the stratum corneum. Their size alone makes penetration through intact skin essentially negligible. This is part of why most protein-based drugs cannot be delivered transdermally.
explanations.C: Correct. Lipid-soluble (lipophilic) molecules dissolve directly into and diffuse through the lipid-rich intercellular matrix of the stratum corneum, the skin's outermost barrier layer. This is the physiological basis for transdermal drug delivery systems, which are deliberately formulated to be lipid-soluble to exploit this route. Small size also helps, but lipid solubility is the dominant factor determining ease of penetration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Polysaccharides are large, hydrophilic carbohydrate molecules that do not dissolve into the lipid matrix and are effectively blocked by the stratum corneum. Their size and water solubility both work against penetration. They behave similarly to large proteins in this respect.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Nucleic acids are large, highly charged, water-soluble molecules that cannot cross the lipid-rich stratum corneum under normal conditions. Their combination of size and charge makes intact-skin penetration essentially impossible without specialised delivery techniques.

questions.learning_objective: State that lipid-soluble molecules penetrate intact skin most readily.
